title: Detection Strategy for Defense Impairment via Prevent Command History Logging across OS platforms.
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Defense Impairment via Prevent Com...
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary attempts to impair defenses by preventing command history logging on Linux, macOS and other Unix-like hosts, which maps to T1690. Command history is one of the few reliable evidential sources for what an intruder typed, so turning it off removes audit evidence and reduces the chance that post-incident review can reconstruct attacker actions. The telemetry that makes this possible includes shell process creation with full command lines, file modification events on shell history and shell startup files, and security audit records for attribute changes to those files. In practice the detection fails for two reasons: short-lived interactive commands are often not collected unless command line auditing is enabled, and legitimate configuration management and hardening scripts also modify history settings, which pushes analysts toward permissive filters.

beginner.definition: This rule looks for signs that command history logging has been switched off. Command history is the file where a shell writes the commands a user typed. When logging stops, the record of what happened on that machine disappears.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who removes the trail makes the later investigation much harder. Analysts may never learn which commands ran or which tools were used. This behaviour is also a warning sign on its own, because normal users have little reason to disable logging. Catching it early gives you a chance to look at the host while evidence still exists.
howItWorks: The agent sends every new process to the central platform, with the full command line and the name of the parent process.
A filter keeps only shells and commands that relate to history settings, such as a shell startup command or a change of the history file variable.
The platform also watches file changes on the history file and its parent directory, including permission and attribute changes.
Each match is tagged with the user, the host name and the parent process that started the shell.
The platform groups these events by host and compares the count with the normal baseline for that host.
It raises an alert when the count is unusual, or when a tool that is not an administrator tool starts the command.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman in a warehouse. His only job is to write down every person who enters and leaves. One evening somebody quietly tells him to stop writing, and then takes goods out of the building. The building still looks normal, and the page simply stays empty. The empty page is the clue, not a missing door or a broken lock.
takeaways: An empty or missing command history is a clue, not proof that nothing happened.
This behaviour removes evidence, so it usually appears next to other suspicious activity.
The alert is strongest on hosts where such a change is never expected.

objectives: Explain why command history logging matters as an evidence source during an incident.
Identify the telemetry that records shell execution and history file changes.
Describe how a rule can separate a normal administrator change from a hiding attempt.
List at least three false positives that produce the same pattern.
Explain what coverage is lost when the rule is scoped to a small asset group.
dataSources: Linux auditd execve records providing the full command line and parent process
Sysmon for Linux event 1 process creation including command line and user
Linux auditd file watch records for changes to shell history files and their directory attributes
macOS unified log entries for shell sessions and profile script execution
Endpoint agent file integrity monitoring alerts for shell history and shell configuration files
logic: The signal is a shell or a short-lived process whose command line relates to history control, such as unsetting or unexporting the history file variable, setting the history size to zero, or making the history file unwritable, appearing together with file change events on that history file. You must correlate the process command line, the parent process, the acting user and the file path, because the same command is normal in an administrative session on a jump host and abnormal on an application server. The malicious case differs from the benign one in frequency and context: it is a one-off, on a host whose baseline has no such change, often immediately before or after discovery activity by the same user.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Command History Logging Disabled by Shell Process
# logsource:
#   product: linux
# detection:
#   selection:
#     type: EXECVE
#     command_line|contains:
#       - 'HISTFILE='
#       - 'HISTSIZE=0'
#       - 'unset HISTFILE'
#       - 'set +o history'
#   condition: selection
# level: medium
falsePositives: Configuration management tools that enforce a hardened shell profile with a reduced history size
Automated backup scripts that temporarily change history file permissions before copying the file
Developers running long batch jobs who disable history to keep the interactive file small
Security assessment teams performing authorized tests on a scoped jump host
tuningNotes: Start by baselining how often these command patterns normally appear per host group, then add a filter that excludes the configuration management service account and the documented hardening change window. Scope the rule to servers that hold sensitive data or host interactive administrator sessions, because build agents and containers generate constant shell noise. Narrowing this way means you may miss an attacker who hides inside the excluded account, so review the exclusion list each quarter and keep a separate low-severity rule that still records, but does not alert on, the excluded account.
